expectedText:
CORPORATE BYLAWS
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE
These are the bylaws of Acme, Inc., a corporation organized under the laws of Delaware. They govern the internal affairs of the corporation until amended as provided below.

SHAREHOLDER MEETINGS
Unless the articles of incorporation say otherwise, a quorum for a shareholders' meeting is a majority of the shares entitled to vote, present in person or by proxy — though it can never be less than one-third of the shares entitled to vote (20% instead, for a mutual water company), and (except for a close corporation) never more than a majority either. Once a quorum is present, a matter passes with the affirmative vote of a majority of the shares actually represented and voting at the meeting, unless a bigger vote is required by law or the articles.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "Unless otherwise provided in the articles, a majority of the shares entitled to vote, represented in person or by proxy, shall constitute a quorum at a meeting of the shareholders, but in no event shall a quorum consist of less than one-third (or, in the case of a mutual water company, 20 percent) of the shares entitled to vote at the meeting or, except in the case of a close corporation, of more than a majority of the shares entitled to vote at the meeting."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 602(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, shareholder meeting quorum floor and ceiling (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=602.)
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), the affirmative vote of a majority of the shares represented and voting at a duly held meeting at which a quorum is present (which shares voting affirmatively also constitute at least a majority of the required quorum) shall be the act of the shareholders, unless the vote of a greater number or voting by classes is required by this division or the articles."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 602(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, shareholder voting threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=602.)
  Known gap: This is one state's default rule, used here as real evidence of what a corporation gets automatically if its own bylaws don't set a different quorum or voting threshold — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. The quorum requirement is boxed in on both sides by statute in this state: bylaws can't set it below one-third (or 20% for a mutual water company), and — unless the corporation is a close corporation — can't set it above a majority either. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 602) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

IF SHAREHOLDERS LEAVE MID-MEETING
Once a quorum is present at a properly called shareholders' meeting, the meeting doesn't automatically lose its authority to act just because enough shareholders leave to drop attendance below quorum. The shareholders who remain may keep transacting business, as long as whatever they approve (other than an adjournment) gets the affirmative vote of at least a majority of the shares it would have taken to make a quorum in the first place — or a bigger vote, if a bigger vote was otherwise required for that action.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "The shareholders present at a duly called or held meeting at which a quorum is present may continue to transact business until adjournment notwithstanding the withdrawal of enough shareholders to leave less than a quorum, if any action taken (other than adjournment) is approved by at least a majority of the shares required to constitute a quorum"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 602(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, meeting continues despite a walkout (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=602.)
  Known gap: This is one state's default rule, used here as real evidence of a genuine feature of shareholder-meeting procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This means a shareholder can't block action simply by walking out once a quorum has already been established; the practical check is the majority-of-quorum vote threshold, not attendance at the moment of the vote. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 602(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

ACTING WITHOUT A MEETING
Shareholders can generally approve most actions in writing, without holding a meeting at all, as long as shareholders holding at least the number of votes it would take to approve that action at a meeting sign a written consent. Electing directors is a real exception to that rule: directors can't be elected by written consent unless every single share entitled to vote signs on — a bare or even large majority isn't enough — with one narrow carve-out: shareholders can fill a board vacancy (other than one created by removing a director) by written consent of a majority of the outstanding voting shares.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "Unless otherwise provided in the articles, any action that may be taken at any annual or special meeting of shareholders may be taken without a meeting and without prior notice, if a consent in writing, as specified in Section 195, setting forth the action so taken, shall be provided by the holders of outstanding shares having not less than the minimum number of votes that would be necessary to authorize or take that action at a meeting at which all shares entitled to vote thereon were present and voted."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 603(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, general written-consent mechanism (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=603.)
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (a), directors may not be elected by written consent except by unanimous written consent of all shares entitled to vote for the election of directors; provided that the shareholders may elect a director to fill a vacancy, other than a vacancy created by removal, by the written consent of a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 603(d) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, directors generally can't be elected by less than unanimous consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=603.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. A shareholder who signs a consent can revoke it, but only before the required number of consents needed to approve the action have actually been filed with the corporation — not after. Separately, unless every voting shareholder consented in writing, the statute requires notice to shareholders who didn't sign, timed differently depending on what kind of action was approved. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 603) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

BOARD OF DIRECTORS
The number of directors shall be _______. Directors are elected by the shareholders at each annual meeting and serve until the next annual meeting or until a successor is elected.

CUMULATIVE VOTING FOR DIRECTORS
Shareholders have a default right to cumulative voting in director elections, subject to certain exceptions (classified boards and short-slate voting under other sections, discussed below): instead of casting one vote per share for each open board seat, a shareholder can give one candidate a number of votes equal to the number of directors being elected multiplied by that shareholder's normal vote count, or spread those same total votes across several candidates as they choose. That right doesn't activate automatically at a given meeting — it requires that a candidate's name was placed in nomination before the voting, and that some shareholder gave notice at the meeting, before voting began, of an intention to cumulate votes. Once any one shareholder gives that notice, every shareholder at that meeting may cumulate their votes.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "Except as provided in Sections 301.5 and 708.5, every shareholder complying with subdivision (b) and entitled to vote at any election of directors may cumulate such shareholder’s votes and give one candidate a number of votes equal to the number of directors to be elected multiplied by the number of votes to which the shareholder’s shares are normally entitled, or distribute the shareholder’s votes on the same principle among as many candidates as the shareholder thinks fit."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 708(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, the cumulative voting mechanism (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=708.)
  "No shareholder shall be entitled to cumulate votes (i.e., cast for any candidate a number of votes greater than the number of votes that the shareholder normally is entitled to cast) unless the candidate or candidates’ names have been placed in nomination prior to the voting and the shareholder has given notice at the meeting prior to the voting of the shareholder’s intention to cumulate the shareholder’s votes. If any one shareholder has given that notice, all shareholders may cumulate their votes for candidates in nomination."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 708(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, the notice precondition for cumulative voting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=708.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default shareholder right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Cumulative voting is a real protection for minority shareholders — it lets a large-enough minority concentrate their votes to elect at least one director, something they generally couldn't do if every seat were decided on a simple one-vote-per-share, highest-vote-getters basis. This right doesn't apply the same way to every corporation: it's subject to two statutory exceptions this document doesn't detail (classified-board and short-slate-voting rules under other sections), and it doesn't apply at all to a mutual water company's shareholders unless that company's own articles or bylaws say it does. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 708) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

REMOVING A DIRECTOR BEFORE THEIR TERM ENDS
Shareholders can generally remove one or more directors without cause, by the same kind of vote it would take to elect them. But that power has a real limit tied directly to cumulative voting: a director can't be removed (unless the whole board is removed at once) if the votes cast against removal would have been enough to elect that director in the first place, assuming they'd been cast cumulatively in an election for the board's full authorized size. A corporation with a classified board is a real exception to that limit — it gets a separate, differently worded cumulative-voting test instead.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "Any or all of the directors may be removed without cause if the removal is approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152), subject to the following: (1) Except for a corporation to which paragraph (3) is applicable, no director may be removed (unless the entire board is removed) when the votes cast against removal, or not consenting in writing to the removal, would be sufficient to elect the director if voted cumulatively at an election at which the same total number of votes were cast (or, if the action is taken by written consent, all shares entitled to vote were voted) and the entire number of directors authorized at the time of the director’s most recent election were then being elected."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 303(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, removal without cause and the cumulative-voting protection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=303.)
  "A director of a corporation whose board of directors is classified pursuant to Section 301.5 may not be removed if the votes cast against removal of the director, or not consenting in writing to the removal, would be sufficient to elect the director if voted cumulatively (without regard to whether shares may otherwise be voted cumulatively) at an election at which the same total number of votes were cast (or, if the action is taken by written consent, all shares entitled to vote were voted) and either the number of directors elected at the most recent annual meeting of shareholders, or if greater, the number of directors for whom removal is being sought, were then being elected."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 303(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, the separate test for a classified board (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=303.)
  "Any reduction of the authorized number of directors or amendment reducing the number of classes of directors does not remove any director prior to the expiration of the director’s term of office."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 303(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, reducing the board doesn't remove a sitting director (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=303.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine minority-shareholder protection — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This protection exists specifically because of cumulative voting: it prevents a bare majority from simply voting out a director whom a large-enough minority elected using their cumulative-voting power, which would otherwise make that minority protection meaningless. Reducing the authorized number of directors, or amending the bylaws to reduce board classes, doesn't itself remove a sitting director before their term is up. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 303) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

BOARD MEETINGS
Unless the bylaws provide otherwise, a majority of the authorized number of directors constitutes a quorum for a board meeting, and a decision made by a majority of the directors present at a meeting where a quorum exists is the act of the board — except for certain interested-director transactions and indemnification decisions covered elsewhere in this same corporate law, which carry their own, different approval requirements a plain majority doesn't automatically satisfy.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "A majority of the authorized number of directors constitutes a quorum of the board for the transaction of business. The articles or bylaws may not provide that a quorum shall be less than one-third the authorized number of directors or less than two, whichever is larger, unless the authorized number of directors is one, in which case one director constitutes a quorum."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(7) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, board meeting quorum (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=307.)
  "An act or decision done or made by a majority of the directors present at a meeting duly held at which a quorum is present is the act of the board, subject to the provisions of Section 310 and subdivision (e) of Section 317."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(8) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, act of the board (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=307.)
  Known gap: This state's statute puts a real floor under how low a corporation can set board quorum by bylaw: never less than one-third of the authorized number of directors, and never less than two — unless the corporation has only one director, in which case that one director is a quorum. The statute also bars the bylaws from letting fewer than a majority of directors present decide a matter; a corporation can require a bigger majority for board decisions, but can't require a smaller one. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence these floors are a genuine feature of corporate law generally, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 307) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

CALLING AND NOTICING BOARD MEETINGS
A regular board meeting can be held without any notice at all, as long as the bylaws or the board have already fixed its time and place. A special meeting is different: it requires at least four days' notice by mail, or 48 hours' notice delivered personally, by telephone (including voicemail), or electronically. Unlike quorum, this is a floor the bylaws can't lower — they cannot do away with notice of a special meeting altogether. Directors don't have to meet in person: participating by conference telephone or video counts as being present, as long as everyone can hear each other.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "Regular meetings of the board may be held without notice if the time and place of the meetings are fixed by the bylaws or the board. Special meetings of the board shall be held upon four days’ notice by mail or 48 hours’ notice delivered personally or by telephone, including a voice messaging system or by electronic transmission by the corporation (Section 20). The articles or bylaws may not dispense with notice of a special meeting."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, notice for regular vs. special board meetings (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=307.)
  "Participation in a meeting through use of conference telephone or electronic video screen communication pursuant to this subdivision constitutes presence in person at that meeting as long as all members participating in the meeting are able to hear one another"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, remote participation counts as presence (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=307.)
  Known gap: This is one state's default rule, used here as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. A director who shows up to a meeting without objecting to a lack of notice, or who signs a written waiver, can't later challenge that meeting for lack of notice — but that's a separate, narrower point from whether notice was required in the first place. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 307) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

OFFICERS
The officers of Acme, Inc. are a president, a secretary, and a treasurer, each appointed by the board of directors and serving at the board's discretion. The same person may hold more than one office. The board may also appoint one or more vice presidents or other officers as it determines necessary.

INDEMNIFICATION
Acme, Inc. may indemnify a director, officer, employee, or other agent who is or was a party to a legal proceeding because of that role, against expenses, judgments, fines, and settlements actually and reasonably incurred, if that person acted in good faith and in a manner reasonably believed to be in the corporation's best interests — and, in a criminal proceeding, had no reasonable cause to believe the conduct was unlawful.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "A corporation shall have power to indemnify any person who was or is a party or is threatened to be made a party to any proceeding (other than an action by or in the right of the corporation to procure a judgment in its favor) by reason of the fact that the person is or was an agent of the corporation, against expenses, judgments, fines, settlements, and other amounts actually and reasonably incurred in connection with the proceeding if that person acted in good faith and in a manner the person reasonably believed to be in the best interests of the corporation and, in the case of a criminal proceeding, had no reasonable cause to believe the conduct of the person was unlawful."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, permissive power to indemnify (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  "No indemnification shall be made under this subdivision for any of the following: (1) In respect of any claim, issue or matter as to which the person shall have been adjudged to be liable to the corporation in the performance of that person’s duty to the corporation and its shareholders, unless and only to the extent that the court in which the proceeding is or was pending shall determine upon application that, in view of all the circumstances of the case, the person is fairly and reasonably entitled to indemnity for expenses and then only to the extent that the court shall determine."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, derivative-suit limitation on indemnification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This power is permissive under this statute — it authorizes indemnification but doesn't by itself require it; a corporation that wants indemnification to be guaranteed, not discretionary, typically has to say so explicitly in its own bylaws or a separate agreement. A real, important limitation: this specific rule is narrower for a proceeding brought by or in the right of the corporation itself (a derivative suit) — indemnification for amounts a person is found liable to the corporation for is barred in that kind of case unless a court specifically determines the person is fairly and reasonably entitled to it, even where the general good-faith standard above would otherwise be met. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what indemnification powers and limits typically look like — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 317) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

WHEN INDEMNIFICATION ISN'T OPTIONAL
Everything above is a power Acme, Inc. may exercise, not a promise — except in one specific situation, where indemnification stops being discretionary: if a director, officer, employee, or other agent is successful on the merits in defending a proceeding (or a specific claim or issue within it), the corporation must indemnify that person for the expenses actually and reasonably incurred defending it.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "To the extent that an agent of a corporation has been successful on the merits in defense of any proceeding referred to in subdivision (b) or (c) or in defense of any claim, issue, or matter therein, the agent shall be indemnified against expenses actually and reasonably incurred by the agent in connection therewith."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(d) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, mandatory indemnification for success on the merits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine mandatory floor underneath the general discretionary indemnification power — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. "Successful on the merits" is a narrower outcome than simply avoiding liability (for example, a case settled or dismissed on procedural grounds may not qualify), so this mandatory right shouldn't be assumed to cover every favorable outcome. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 317(d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

ADVANCING DEFENSE COSTS
Acme, Inc. may pay a director, officer, employee, or other agent's litigation expenses as they're incurred, before the proceeding is even over, rather than waiting to reimburse them only after a final determination that indemnification is proper. That advance comes with a condition: the person receiving it must first agree, in writing, to repay the money if it turns out later that they weren't actually entitled to be indemnified.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "Expenses incurred in defending any proceeding may be advanced by the corporation prior to the final disposition of the proceeding upon receipt of an undertaking by or on behalf of the agent to repay that amount if it shall be determined ultimately that the agent is not entitled to be indemnified as authorized in this section."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(f) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, advancement of defense expenses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Like the general indemnification power itself, advancement here is something the corporation may do, not something it automatically must do, unless the corporation's own bylaws or a separate agreement commits to it. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 317(f)); no additional independent source was found for this.

AMENDMENT
These bylaws may be amended by the affirmative vote of a majority of the directors then in office, or by the affirmative vote of a majority of the shares entitled to vote, unless the articles of incorporation or applicable law require a greater vote for a specific amendment.

ADOPTION
Adopted by the board of directors of Acme, Inc.:

Director: _______________________ Date: _______________
Director: _______________________ Date: _______________
(Add additional signature lines as needed.)

But that power has a real limit tied directly to cumulative voting: a director can't be removed (unless the whole board is removed at once) if the votes cast against removal would have been enough to elect that director in the first place, assuming they'd been cast cumulatively in an election for the board's full authorized size. A corporation with a classified board is a real exception to that limit — it gets a separate, differently worded cumulative-voting test instead.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 303(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, removal without cause and the cumulative-voting protection
citations.quote: Any or all of the directors may be removed without cause if the removal is approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152), subject to the following: (1) Except for a corporation to which paragraph (3) is applicable, no director may be removed (unless the entire board is removed) when the votes cast against removal, or not consenting in writing to the removal, would be sufficient to elect the director if voted cumulatively at an election at which the same total number of votes were cast (or, if the action is taken by written consent, all shares entitled to vote were voted) and the entire number of directors authorized at the time of the director’s most recent election were then being elected.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 303(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the separate test for a classified board
citations.quote: A director of a corporation whose board of directors is classified pursuant to Section 301.5 may not be removed if the votes cast against removal of the director, or not consenting in writing to the removal, would be sufficient to elect the director if voted cumulatively (without regard to whether shares may otherwise be voted cumulatively) at an election at which the same total number of votes were cast (or, if the action is taken by written consent, all shares entitled to vote were voted) and either the number of directors elected at the most recent annual meeting of shareholders, or if greater, the number of directors for whom removal is being sought, were then being elected.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 303(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, reducing the board doesn't remove a sitting director
citations.quote: Any reduction of the authorized number of directors or amendment reducing the number of classes of directors does not remove any director prior to the expiration of the director’s term of office.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine minority-shareholder protection — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This protection exists specifically because of cumulative voting: it prevents a bare majority from simply voting out a director whom a large-enough minority elected using their cumulative-voting power, which would otherwise make that minority protection meaningless. Reducing the authorized number of directors, or amending the bylaws to reduce board classes, doesn't itself remove a sitting director before their term is up. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 303) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: Unless the bylaws provide otherwise, a majority of the authorized number of directors constitutes a quorum for a board meeting, and a decision made by a majority of the directors present at a meeting where a quorum exists is the act of the board — except for certain interested-director transactions and indemnification decisions covered elsewhere in this same corporate law, which carry their own, different approval requirements a plain majority doesn't automatically satisfy.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(7) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, board meeting quorum
citations.quote: A majority of the authorized number of directors constitutes a quorum of the board for the transaction of business. The articles or bylaws may not provide that a quorum shall be less than one-third the authorized number of directors or less than two, whichever is larger, unless the authorized number of directors is one, in which case one director constitutes a quorum.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(8) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, act of the board
citations.quote: An act or decision done or made by a majority of the directors present at a meeting duly held at which a quorum is present is the act of the board, subject to the provisions of Section 310 and subdivision (e) of Section 317.

expectedJSON.gap: This state's statute puts a real floor under how low a corporation can set board quorum by bylaw: never less than one-third of the authorized number of directors, and never less than two — unless the corporation has only one director, in which case that one director is a quorum. The statute also bars the bylaws from letting fewer than a majority of directors present decide a matter; a corporation can require a bigger majority for board decisions, but can't require a smaller one. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence these floors are a genuine feature of corporate law generally, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 307) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: A regular board meeting can be held without any notice at all, as long as the bylaws or the board have already fixed its time and place. A special meeting is different: it requires at least four days' notice by mail, or 48 hours' notice delivered personally, by telephone (including voicemail), or electronically. Unlike quorum, this is a floor the bylaws can't lower — they cannot do away with notice of a special meeting altogether. Directors don't have to meet in person: participating by conference telephone or video counts as being present, as long as everyone can hear each other.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, notice for regular vs. special board meetings
citations.quote: Regular meetings of the board may be held without notice if the time and place of the meetings are fixed by the bylaws or the board. Special meetings of the board shall be held upon four days’ notice by mail or 48 hours’ notice delivered personally or by telephone, including a voice messaging system or by electronic transmission by the corporation (Section 20). The articles or bylaws may not dispense with notice of a special meeting.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 307(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, remote participation counts as presence
citations.quote: Participation in a meeting through use of conference telephone or electronic video screen communication pursuant to this subdivision constitutes presence in person at that meeting as long as all members participating in the meeting are able to hear one another

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's default rule, used here as real evidence of a genuine formal requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. A director who shows up to a meeting without objecting to a lack of notice, or who signs a written waiver, can't later challenge that meeting for lack of notice — but that's a separate, narrower point from whether notice was required in the first place. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 307) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: The officers of Acme, Inc. are a president, a secretary, and a treasurer, each appointed by the board of directors and serving at the board's discretion. The same person may hold more than one office. The board may also appoint one or more vice presidents or other officers as it determines necessary.

Acme, Inc. may indemnify a director, officer, employee, or other agent who is or was a party to a legal proceeding because of that role, against expenses, judgments, fines, and settlements actually and reasonably incurred, if that person acted in good faith and in a manner reasonably believed to be in the corporation's best interests — and, in a criminal proceeding, had no reasonable cause to believe the conduct was unlawful.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, permissive power to indemnify
citations.quote: A corporation shall have power to indemnify any person who was or is a party or is threatened to be made a party to any proceeding (other than an action by or in the right of the corporation to procure a judgment in its favor) by reason of the fact that the person is or was an agent of the corporation, against expenses, judgments, fines, settlements, and other amounts actually and reasonably incurred in connection with the proceeding if that person acted in good faith and in a manner the person reasonably believed to be in the best interests of the corporation and, in the case of a criminal proceeding, had no reasonable cause to believe the conduct of the person was unlawful.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, derivative-suit limitation on indemnification
citations.quote: No indemnification shall be made under this subdivision for any of the following: (1) In respect of any claim, issue or matter as to which the person shall have been adjudged to be liable to the corporation in the performance of that person’s duty to the corporation and its shareholders, unless and only to the extent that the court in which the proceeding is or was pending shall determine upon application that, in view of all the circumstances of the case, the person is fairly and reasonably entitled to indemnity for expenses and then only to the extent that the court shall determine.

expectedJSON.gap: This power is permissive under this statute — it authorizes indemnification but doesn't by itself require it; a corporation that wants indemnification to be guaranteed, not discretionary, typically has to say so explicitly in its own bylaws or a separate agreement. A real, important limitation: this specific rule is narrower for a proceeding brought by or in the right of the corporation itself (a derivative suit) — indemnification for amounts a person is found liable to the corporation for is barred in that kind of case unless a court specifically determines the person is fairly and reasonably entitled to it, even where the general good-faith standard above would otherwise be met. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what indemnification powers and limits typically look like — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 317) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: Everything above is a power Acme, Inc. may exercise, not a promise — except in one specific situation, where indemnification stops being discretionary: if a director, officer, employee, or other agent is successful on the merits in defending a proceeding (or a specific claim or issue within it), the corporation must indemnify that person for the expenses actually and reasonably incurred defending it.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, mandatory indemnification for success on the merits
citations.quote: To the extent that an agent of a corporation has been successful on the merits in defense of any proceeding referred to in subdivision (b) or (c) or in defense of any claim, issue, or matter therein, the agent shall be indemnified against expenses actually and reasonably incurred by the agent in connection therewith.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine mandatory floor underneath the general discretionary indemnification power — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. "Successful on the merits" is a narrower outcome than simply avoiding liability (for example, a case settled or dismissed on procedural grounds may not qualify), so this mandatory right shouldn't be assumed to cover every favorable outcome. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 317(d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: Acme, Inc. may pay a director, officer, employee, or other agent's litigation expenses as they're incurred, before the proceeding is even over, rather than waiting to reimburse them only after a final determination that indemnification is proper. That advance comes with a condition: the person receiving it must first agree, in writing, to repay the money if it turns out later that they weren't actually entitled to be indemnified.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, advancement of defense expenses
citations.quote: Expenses incurred in defending any proceeding may be advanced by the corporation prior to the final disposition of the proceeding upon receipt of an undertaking by or on behalf of the agent to repay that amount if it shall be determined ultimately that the agent is not entitled to be indemnified as authorized in this section.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Like the general indemnification power itself, advancement here is something the corporation may do, not something it automatically must do, unless the corporation's own bylaws or a separate agreement commits to it. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 317(f)); no additional independent source was found for this.
